nameStory: The 'roundleaf' part of this greenbrier's name comes from its distinctively circular to heart-shaped leaves, which stand out among the more elongated leaves of its relatives. 'Greenbrier' refers to the green stems armed with sharp thorns that can snag clothing and skin - definitely living up to the 'brier' reputation! In some southern areas, people call it 'bamboo vine' because of its green, segmented-looking stems.
description: Roundleaf greenbrier is a woody climbing vine that uses curly tendrils to scramble up trees and shrubs throughout New England's forests. Its glossy, circular to heart-shaped leaves and green stems covered in sharp spines make it easy to spot - and unfortunately, easy to get caught on! This native vine produces small greenish-white flowers in late spring and summer, followed by dark blue-black berries in fall. It's a common sight in woodlands, where it can climb quite high into the forest canopy.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Glossy green leaves that are distinctly round to heart-shaped, feeling smooth and leathery to the touch, measuring roughly 2-5 inches long with prominent veins

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbing woody vine that uses green, curly tendrils sprouting directly from the leaf stems (petioles) to grip and climb other plants

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Green, rounded stems armed with sharp, needle-like spines that can easily pierce clothing and skin - handle with care!

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish-white flowers in small clusters, not particularly showy but fragrant up close during late spring and summer

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark blue-black berries about the size of small blueberries, ripening in September and often persisting into winter

habitat: Roundleaf greenbrier thrives in New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly in areas with rich, moist soils. You'll commonly find it climbing through understory shrubs and up into tree canopies, especially in oak-hickory forests, along woodland edges, and in areas with partial shade. It's adaptable and can handle various soil types, from sandy to clay.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green and tender, with the distinctive round shape becoming apparent. Curly tendrils actively seek new supports as the vine begins its climbing growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full, glossy foliage and small greenish-white flowers blooming from April through August. The vine reaches maximum height and leaf coverage.
seasonality.fall: Dark blue-black berries ripen in September, creating an important food source for wildlife. Leaves may turn yellow before dropping, revealing the thorny green stems.
seasonality.winter: Leafless green stems with prominent spines remain visible, often still climbing high into bare trees. Persistent berries may remain on the vine, and the thorny stems become more obvious.

funFact: The young shoots and leaves of roundleaf greenbrier are actually edible and taste surprisingly like asparagus when cooked - despite those intimidating thorns, this 'pest' plant was historically an important wild food source for Indigenous peoples and early settlers!
confusionNotes: Roundleaf greenbrier's circular leaves make it fairly distinctive, but it can be confused with other greenbrier species. Remember: if the leaves are truly round to heart-shaped (not elongated), you've got roundleaf greenbrier. The thorny stems separate it from the smooth-stemmed carrionflower, which also has rounder leaves but lacks spines entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Many people consider greenbriers to be nuisance plants because of their aggressive climbing habit and painful thorns, but they're actually valuable native species that provide important wildlife food and nesting sites. The berries feed over 40 species of birds, and the dense tangles offer excellent cover for small animals.
compareHints: Roundleaf greenbrier stands out from its relatives by its distinctly circular to heart-shaped leaves - sawbrier and saw greenbrier have more elongated, oval leaves. Unlike smooth carrionflower, which has similar round leaves, roundleaf greenbrier has those characteristic sharp spines along its green stems. The woody nature of its stems also distinguishes it from the herbaceous (non-woody) carrionflower.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's greenbriers, sawbrier stands out for its distinctly pale, whitish leaf undersides - roundleaf greenbrier lacks this feature and has rounder leaves, while smooth carrionflower is herbaceous (not woody) and lacks thorns entirely.
Unlike roundleaf greenbrier and sawbrier, smooth carrionflower lacks thorns entirely and dies back to the ground each winter rather than remaining woody year-round.
Saw greenbrier differs from roundleaf greenbrier by its distinctly flattened, saw-toothed prickles rather than straight thorns, and its thicker, more leathery leaves.
